newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to crack down on loan defaulters.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to crack down on loan defaulters.

text.p: Bangladesh, spurred by the World Bank, has launched a programme to recover 1,500 billion taka ($35 billion) in overdue bank loans, the head of the central bank said on Wednesday.
Lutfar Rahman Sarkar, governor of Bangladesh Bank, said a crackdown on defaulters had been recommended by the World Bank, which also urged the government to restructure the financial sector.

A World Bank report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, said that a "bankruptcy act, and badly needed amendments to the Financial Loan Courts Act to deal with loan defaulters remained unapproved for over a year. (As a result) the condition of the domestic private banks worsened."
Bangladesh's parliament last month passed the loan courts act amendments but officials said they had yet to take effect.
The legislation would allow loan courts to send defaulters to jail and make them forfeit their property.
The rate of default on credit from private sector banks is 48 percent, from public sector banks 35 percent and from development financial institutions 90 percent.
Sarkar said several steps had been taken to increase loan recovery and stop defaulters from seeking more bank money.

"All the lending banks have been asked to realise at least 50 percent of their overdue loans by end of March, 1997," he told Reuters. A task force had been formed in the central bank to monitor progress.
Sarkar listed other steps to prevent defaults.
He said the worthiness of borrowers would be examined carefully along with the viability of projects before approval of credit.
Each bank will create a monitoring department for strong supervision of loan recovery.

Finally, he said, borrowers would be awarded rebates for good performance and regular payment of instalments. Bank officials who performed well would be rewarded with cash, increments, promotion and training at home and abroad, Sarkar said.
A committee, which includes Sarkar, has suggested the government form a consortium with commercial banks for giving credit to big projects.
It also recommended against waiving interest on credit except for special cases and against rescheduling loans more than twice, one committee member told Reuters.
The committee proposed that a loan court be set up in each of 64 administrative districts for quick disposal of about 50,000 pending loan cases.
The expenses of the courts would be met with a percentage of money recovered.
